summary: Reports which ARPANET sites Rand had contacted by July 15, 1971, and which network software elements had been verified at each. The matrix covers items such as the NCP, ICP, Telnet user and server programs and the log-on procedure.

eli5.summary: A report card listing which sites have passed which tests, such as can they talk, can they connect, can they log in.

questions: which arpanet sites were checked in july 1971
subtitle: A July 1971 scoreboard of which early ARPANET sites had passed which software checks.

tldr.problem: As sites joined the network, someone needed to track which of them actually worked with the network software.
tldr.mechanism: The authors at Rand list the sites they had contacted by 15 July and mark in a matrix which software elements they had verified at each, with notes on problems.
tldr.outcome: It is a status snapshot, not a protocol. The unit metadata lists RFC 198 as an update to it.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 198 as an update to this report and gives its status as unknown. It is a snapshot of July 1971 and not a specification.

sections.title: What Was Checked
sections.content:
As of 15 July 1971, the Rand authors had contacted, or been contacted by, ten sites: SDC, UCLA-91, UCLA-S7, SRI-10, UCSB, MIT-10, MIT-645, LL-67, BBN-10 and UTAH. The matrix marks which elements of network software they had verified at each site.

The columns are NCP-1, two ICP columns labelled 107 and 80, user Telnet, server Telnet, a Telnet-like protocol, the log-on procedure and accessed services. An x means the element was verified. MIT-645 is marked only as partial.
sections.eli5: The authors made a grid with the computers down the side and the tests across the top, and put an x where a computer passed.

sections.title: Results by Site
sections.content:
UCLA-S7 has the most marks of any site, seven of the eight columns, followed by UCSB with five, including the log-on procedure and accessed services. BBN-10 has the Telnet-like protocol, log-on and accessed services marked. SDC has only NCP-1.

For LL-67, the authors were told by Joel Winett that NCP, ICP, EBCDIC, Telnet and access to a virtual 360 were working, but hardware difficulties meant they had not verified this. For MIT-645, they understood most software worked but had not verified it. UTAH had been tested before TENEX, which was then being installed.
sections.eli5: Some computers passed nearly every test, some passed one or two, and for a couple the authors had only been told it worked and had not seen it themselves.

sections.title: Problems Noted
sections.content:
At SRI-10 the Telnet-like protocol ended lines with X'0D' rather than X'0D0A', which differs from Telnet. John Melvin was to have it fixed. BBN-10 showed the same difference, and under certain conditions its ICP generated a zero byte size. Ray Tomlinson said these quirks would be fixed in about a week.

Three sites commented that TENEX assigns the same local socket to multiple connections when acting as a server. Ray said this is the design, not an error. BBN TENEX was already being used productively via the Net for some non-network problems.
sections.eli5: A couple of computers ended their lines in a slightly different way than the rule book says, and the owners promised to fix it soon.
